topics.name: How the brain works
topics.description: Neurons, brain anatomy, neuroplasticity, brain development, basic neuroscience lectures, how memories or thoughts are physically implemented.

topics.name: Perception & illusions
topics.description: Vision, hearing, touch, optical and auditory illusions, color perception, face recognition, synesthesia, how the brain constructs reality.

topics.name: Sleep & dreams
topics.description: Sleep science, circadian rhythms, insomnia, dreaming, lucid dreams, naps, Matthew Walker, sleep deprivation.

topics.name: Dopamine, hormones & neurochemistry
topics.description: Dopamine, serotonin, oxytocin, cortisol, testosterone, caffeine, alcohol and drugs on the brain, Huberman-style protocols, reward systems.

topics.name: Brain injury, dementia & neurological cases
topics.description: Stroke, split-brain patients, aphasia, amnesia, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Oliver Sacks-style case studies, blindness and the brain.

topics.name: Brain-computer interfaces & neuroimaging
topics.description: BCIs, Neuralink, fMRI, EEG, optogenetics, brain organoids, reading thoughts with machines, neurotechnology.

topics.name: Animal minds & behavior
topics.description: Animal cognition, crows and octopuses, primate studies, ethology, animal emotions, Pavlov and Skinner's animals, comparative psychology.

topics.name: Memory
topics.description: How memory works, forgetting, false memories, Loftus, eyewitness memory, memory palaces, mnemonics, spaced repetition, superior memory.

topics.name: Attention, focus & distraction
topics.description: Attention, multitasking, flow, deep work, procrastination mechanics, boredom, inattentional blindness, the gorilla experiment.

topics.name: Learning how to learn
topics.description: Study techniques, retrieval practice, deliberate practice, learning styles myth, how to learn anything, Feynman technique, note-taking, education science.

topics.name: Intelligence, expertise & talent
topics.description: IQ, g factor, Flynn effect, expertise research, 10,000 hours debate, prodigies, savants, chess masters, genius, the limits of talent.

topics.name: Creativity & insight
topics.description: Creative thinking, insight problems, daydreaming, divergent thinking, where ideas come from, the creative process.

topics.name: Language & thought
topics.description: Psycholinguistics, language acquisition, Chomsky vs Skinner, linguistic relativity, bilingual brains, reading, inner speech, how words shape thinking.

topics.name: Biases, heuristics & rationality
topics.description: Cognitive biases, Kahneman and Tversky, Dunning-Kruger, confirmation bias, motivated reasoning, overconfidence, fallacies, how to think better.

topics.name: Decisions, risk & behavioral economics
topics.description: Decision making, prospect theory, loss aversion, nudges, Thaler, Ariely, incentives, gambling and risk perception, choice overload, game theory of people.

topics.name: Conformity, obedience & classic experiments
topics.description: Milgram, Asch, Stanford Prison Experiment, bystander effect, Robbers Cave, the famous social experiments and what they really showed.

topics.name: Persuasion, propaganda & manipulation
topics.description: Cialdini, influence tactics, advertising psychology, propaganda, brainwashing, cults, gaslighting, con artists, Bernays.

topics.name: Morality, altruism & cooperation
topics.description: Moral psychology, Haidt, trolley problems, altruism, cooperation, trust, fairness, empathy, evolution of morality, honesty and cheating.

topics.name: Groups, identity & prejudice
topics.description: In-groups and out-groups, stereotypes, implicit bias, tribalism, polarization, crowd behavior, mobs, identity and belonging.

topics.name: Love, relationships & attachment
topics.description: Attachment theory, romantic love, dating, marriage research, Gottman, friendship, loneliness in relationships, breakups, jealousy, sex and intimacy.

topics.name: Social media, screens & the attention economy
topics.description: Smartphone and social media effects, persuasive design, dark patterns, dopamine loops, screen time, online outrage, porn and the brain, gaming psychology.

topics.name: Depression & anxiety
topics.description: Depression, anxiety disorders, panic, OCD, phobias, rumination, the science of mood disorders, Sapolsky on depression.

topics.name: ADHD, autism & neurodiversity
topics.description: ADHD, autism spectrum, dyslexia, executive function, Russell Barkley, neurodivergent experience, diagnosis debates.

topics.name: Stress, trauma & burnout
topics.description: Stress physiology, cortisol, PTSD, trauma and the body, resilience, burnout, adverse childhood experiences, Zebras don't get ulcers.

topics.name: Addiction & compulsion
topics.description: Substance addiction, behavioral addictions, gambling, Rat Park, dopamine and craving, recovery, harm reduction, nicotine, alcohol dependence.

topics.name: Psychotherapy & how it works
topics.description: CBT, DBT, ACT, psychoanalysis, Freud and Jung, humanistic therapy, Rogers, what therapy does, how to find a therapist, therapist demonstrations, NVC.

topics.name: Psychiatry & medication
topics.description: Antidepressants, SSRIs, antipsychotics, lithium, ketamine as treatment, electroconvulsive therapy, psychiatric diagnosis, DSM debates, history of asylums.

topics.name: Psychedelics & altered states
topics.description: Psilocybin, LSD, MDMA therapy, ketamine, hallucinations, near-death and out-of-body experiences, hypnosis, trance, altered states research.

topics.name: Mindfulness & meditation
topics.description: Meditation science, mindfulness-based stress reduction, Kabat-Zinn, contemplative neuroscience, breathing practices, Wim Hof, Buddhist psychology.

topics.name: Schizophrenia, bipolar & psychosis
topics.description: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, psychosis, dissociation, personality disorders, first-person accounts, severe mental illness and its treatment.

topics.name: Emotions & feelings
topics.description: What emotions are, Lisa Feldman Barrett, Ekman, facial expressions, anger, fear, disgust, shame, emotional regulation, affective neuroscience.

topics.name: Motivation, willpower & habits
topics.description: Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation, Drive, self-determination theory, habit formation, willpower, ego depletion, procrastination, goal setting, discipline.

topics.name: Happiness, meaning & the good life
topics.description: Positive psychology, Seligman, hedonic adaptation, Harvard happiness study, gratitude, flow, Frankl and meaning, status anxiety, wellbeing science.

topics.name: Grief, loneliness & connection
topics.description: Grief and bereavement, loneliness epidemic, social connection and health, belonging, mortality awareness, death and the psyche.

topics.name: Child development
topics.description: Infant cognition, Piaget, attachment in infancy, still-face experiment, theory of mind development, language development, marshmallow test, childhood.

topics.name: Parenting
topics.description: Parenting research and advice grounded in psychology, ADHD parenting, discipline, play, screen rules for kids, raising resilient children.

topics.name: Adolescence & aging
topics.description: Teenage brain, adolescent risk-taking, puberty, cognitive aging, wisdom, dementia prevention, the psychology of old age, life stages.

topics.name: Personality & individual differences
topics.description: Big Five, Myers-Briggs critique, introversion and extraversion, narcissism, psychopathy, dark triad, temperament, personality change, Jordan Peterson personality lectures.

topics.name: Sex, gender & evolutionary psychology
topics.description: Sex differences research, gender psychology, mating psychology, evolutionary psychology of behavior, sexual orientation research, the gender equality paradox debate.

topics.name: Nature, nurture & behavioral genetics
topics.description: Heritability, twin studies, Plomin, epigenetics, genes and intelligence, genes and personality, the nature-nurture debate, Sapolsky on behavior's causes.

topics.name: Consciousness & the self
topics.description: Theories of consciousness, the hard problem, Dennett, Chalmers, qualia, the self as illusion, global workspace, integrated information, anesthesia and awareness.

topics.name: Free will & agency
topics.description: Free will debates, Libet experiments, determinism and responsibility, Sapolsky's Determined, Sam Harris, compatibilism, moral responsibility.

topics.name: Artificial minds & cognitive science
topics.description: Cognitive science, Hofstadter and analogy, computational theories of mind, whether machines can think, Chinese room, embodied cognition, predictive processing, Joscha Bach.

topics.name: Replication crisis & research methods
topics.description: The replication crisis in psychology, p-hacking, power posing collapse, priming failures, statistics for psychology, how to read a study, open science.

topics.name: History of psychology & psychiatry
topics.description: Freud, Jung, Skinner, Wundt, James, the history of psychiatry, lobotomy, asylums, MK-Ultra, the Century of the Self, how psychology became a science.

topics.name: Pseudoscience, cults & belief
topics.description: Why people believe weird things, conspiracy theories, cults, flat earth, pseudoscience in psychology, cognitive dissonance, critical thinking, skepticism.

topics.name: Psychological research & careers
topics.description: What psychologists actually do, graduate school, research design, famous psychologists interviewed, how studies are run, academia in psychology.

topics.name: Work, leadership & organizations
topics.description: Industrial-organizational psychology, motivation at work, leadership, team dynamics, negotiation psychology, meetings and productivity science, remote work and wellbeing.

topics.name: Education & teaching
topics.description: Teaching methods grounded in psychology, classroom learning, educational psychology, growth mindset debate, school and child outcomes, tutoring.

topics.name: Crime, deception & forensic psychology
topics.description: Criminal psychology, interrogation and false confessions, lie detection, serial killers, violence, forensic psychiatry, eyewitness testimony in court.

topics.name: Design, games & behavior
topics.description: Psychology of design and UX, game psychology and player motivation, gamification, choice architecture in products, Don Norman, human factors.

topics.name: Performance, sport & peak states
topics.description: Sport psychology, choking under pressure, flow in performance, public speaking anxiety, visualization, mental training, breathing for performance.

contested_findings.name: Power posing
contested_findings.note: The 2010 power-posing hormone and risk-taking effects did not replicate; co-author Dana Carney disavowed them in 2016. A smaller 'felt power' self-report effect may survive.
contested_findings.source: Simmons & Simonsohn (2017) p-curve; Ranehill et al. (2015) replication

sources.cite: Ranehill et al. (2015). Assessing the robustness of power posing. Psychological Science, 26(5), 653–656.
Simmons & Simonsohn (2017). Power posing: P-curving the evidence. Psychological Science, 28(5), 687–693.

contested_findings.name: Stanford Prison Experiment
contested_findings.note: Archival recordings show guards were coached to be cruel and a key 'breakdown' was reportedly acted; the study is now widely seen as a demonstration, not an experiment.
contested_findings.source: Le Texier (2019) American Psychologist; Blum (2018)

sources.cite: Le Texier, T. (2019). Debunking the Stanford Prison Experiment. American Psychologist, 74(7), 823–839.

contested_findings.name: Marshmallow test
contested_findings.note: A 2018 conceptual replication with a larger, more diverse sample found the link between delay of gratification and later outcomes was much smaller and mostly explained by family background.
contested_findings.source: Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018) Psychological Science

sources.cite: Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018). Revisiting the marshmallow test. Psychological Science, 29(7), 1159–1177.

contested_findings.name: Ego depletion / willpower as a muscle
contested_findings.note: A 2016 multi-lab preregistered replication (23 labs) found an effect indistinguishable from zero.
contested_findings.source: Hagger et al. (2016) Perspectives on Psychological Science

sources.cite: Hagger et al. (2016). A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546–573.

contested_findings.name: Social priming (elderly-words walking, money priming)
contested_findings.note: Classic behavioral priming studies have failed repeated high-powered replications; Kahneman himself urged the field to clean up its act in 2012.
contested_findings.source: Doyen et al. (2012); Many Labs; Kahneman open letter (2012)

sources.cite: Doyen, Klein, Pichon & Cleeremans (2012). Behavioral priming: It's all in the mind, but whose mind? PLOS ONE, 7(1), e29081.
Rohrer, Pashler & Harris (2015). Do subtle reminders of money change people's political views? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(4), e73–e85.

contested_findings.name: Facial feedback (pen-in-teeth)
contested_findings.note: A 17-lab registered replication found no effect of the pen-in-mouth smile manipulation on humor ratings, though later meta-analyses find small effects under some conditions.
contested_findings.source: Wagenmakers et al. (2016) RRR; Coles et al. (2019)

sources.cite: Wagenmakers et al. (2016). Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin & Stepper (1988). Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(6), 917–928.
Coles et al. (2022). A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration. Nature Human Behaviour, 6, 1731–1742.

contested_findings.name: Growth mindset interventions
contested_findings.note: Effects on achievement are real but small (d ≈ 0.1) and concentrated among lower-achieving students; early claims of large effects were overstated.
contested_findings.source: Sisk et al. (2018) meta-analysis; Yeager et al. (2019) Nature

sources.cite: Sisk et al. (2018). To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Psychological Science, 29(4), 549–571.
Yeager et al. (2019). A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement. Nature, 573, 364–369.

contested_findings.name: Learning styles
contested_findings.note: No credible evidence that matching teaching to a student's 'learning style' improves learning; it is considered a neuromyth.
contested_findings.source: Pashler et al. (2008) Psychological Science in the Public Interest

sources.cite: Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer & Bjork (2008). Learning styles: Concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105–119.

contested_findings.name: 10,000-hour rule
contested_findings.note: Deliberate practice explains a minority of the variance in expert performance (about 1–26% depending on domain); the round number is Gladwell's, not Ericsson's finding.
contested_findings.source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014) Psychological Science

sources.cite: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1608–1618.

contested_findings.name: Grit
contested_findings.note: Grit overlaps heavily with conscientiousness and predicts outcomes only modestly beyond it; the original claims were larger than meta-analytic estimates.
contested_findings.source: Credé, Tynan & Harms (2017) JPSP

sources.cite: Credé, Tynan & Harms (2017). Much ado about grit: A meta-analytic synthesis of the grit literature. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113(3), 492–511.

contested_findings.name: Left-brained / right-brained people
contested_findings.note: Hemispheric specialization is real, but there is no evidence people are dominated by one hemisphere in personality or thinking style.
contested_findings.source: Nielsen et al. (2013) PLOS ONE

sources.cite: Nielsen et al. (2013). An evaluation of the left-brain vs. right-brain hypothesis with resting state functional connectivity MRI. PLOS ONE, 8(8), e71275.

contested_findings.name: Milgram obedience (nuance)
contested_findings.note: The headline 65% figure comes from one of ~24 conditions; archival work shows many participants disbelieved the shocks were real, and compliance varied widely across variants. The core effect is not debunked.
contested_findings.source: Perry (2013) Behind the Shock Machine; Haslam & Reicher

sources.cite: Burger, J. M. (2009). Replicating Milgram: Would people still obey today? American Psychologist, 64(1), 1–11.
Haslam & Reicher (2012). Contesting the "nature" of conformity: What Milgram and Zimbardo's studies really show. PLOS Biology, 10(11), e1001426.

contested_findings.name: Kitty Genovese / 38 witnesses story
contested_findings.note: The '38 witnesses who did nothing' account was largely a New York Times myth; some neighbors did call police or shout. The bystander effect itself is a real but context-dependent finding.
contested_findings.source: Manning, Levine & Collins (2007) American Psychologist

sources.cite: Manning, Levine & Collins (2007). The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping. American Psychologist, 62(6), 555–562.

contested_findings.name: Dunning-Kruger effect (debate)
contested_findings.note: Part of the classic pattern can be reproduced from random noise plus regression to the mean; the size and interpretation of the effect are debated, though the pattern is not purely artifactual.
contested_findings.source: Nuhfer et al. (2016, 2017); Gignac & Zajenkowski (2020)

sources.cite: Gignac & Zajenkowski (2020). The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact. Intelligence, 80, 101449.

contested_findings.name: Implicit Association Test as a predictor
contested_findings.note: The IAT has low test-retest reliability and weakly predicts discriminatory behavior; its creators now describe it as unsuited for diagnosing individuals.
contested_findings.source: Oswald et al. (2013); Forscher et al. (2019) meta-analysis

sources.cite: Oswald et al. (2013). Predicting ethnic and racial discrimination: A meta-analysis of IAT criterion studies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 105(2), 171–192.
Forscher et al. (2019). A meta-analysis of procedures to change implicit measures. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 117(3), 522–559.

contested_findings.name: Mozart effect
contested_findings.note: Listening to Mozart does not make you smarter; the original brief spatial-reasoning effect is small, short-lived and reproducible with any arousing music.
contested_findings.source: Pietschnig, Voracek & Formann (2010) meta-analysis

sources.cite: Pietschnig, Voracek & Formann (2010). Mozart effect–Shmozart effect: A meta-analysis. Intelligence, 38(3), 314–323.

contested_findings.name: Little Albert
contested_findings.note: Watson's conditioning demonstration had one subject, no controls, and the baby's identity and health are disputed; it is a historical landmark rather than solid evidence.
contested_findings.source: Harris (1979); Beck, Levinson & Irons (2009); Powell et al. (2014)

sources.cite: Beck, Levinson & Irons (2009). Finding Little Albert. American Psychologist, 64(7), 605–614.
Powell, Digdon, Harris & Smithson (2014). Correcting the record on Watson, Rayner, and Little Albert. American Psychologist, 69(6), 600–611.

contested_findings.name: Chemical imbalance theory of depression
contested_findings.note: A 2022 umbrella review found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin; antidepressants can still work without that explanation being true.
contested_findings.source: Moncrieff et al. (2022) Molecular Psychiatry

sources.cite: Moncrieff et al. (2023). The serotonin theory of depression: A systematic umbrella review of the evidence. Molecular Psychiatry, 28, 3243–3256.

contested_findings.name: Stereotype threat (women and math)
contested_findings.note: Large preregistered replications found little or no stereotype-threat effect on women's math performance; publication bias inflated the early literature.
contested_findings.source: Flore & Wicherts (2015); Flore, Mulder & Wicherts (2018)

sources.cite: Flore & Wicherts (2015). Does stereotype threat influence performance of girls in stereotyped domains? A meta-analysis. Journal of School Psychology, 53(1), 25–44.

Flore, Mulder & Wicherts (2018). The influence of gender stereotype threat on mathematics test scores of Dutch high school students: A registered report. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology, 3(2), 140–174.

contested_findings.name: Mirror neurons explain empathy/autism
contested_findings.note: Mirror neurons exist in monkeys, but the 'broken mirror' theory of autism and claims that they explain empathy or language are not supported.
contested_findings.source: Hickok (2014) The Myth of Mirror Neurons; Hamilton (2013)

sources.cite: Hamilton, A. F. de C. (2013). Reflecting on the mirror neuron system in autism: A systematic review of current theories. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience, 3, 91–105.

contested_findings.name: Huberman protocols (overreach)
contested_findings.note: Popular mechanistic protocols (sunlight timing, cold exposure, supplements) often extrapolate from small or animal studies; the physiology is real, the certainty is not.
contested_findings.source: Critiques in Slate, Scientific American and by sleep researchers (2023–2024)

contested_findings.name: Porn 'addiction' as brain disease
contested_findings.note: Claims that porn rewires the brain like a drug and causes erectile dysfunction come largely from advocacy, not controlled research; evidence for 'porn-induced ED' is weak and moral disapproval predicts self-reported 'addiction' better than use does.
contested_findings.source: Grubbs et al. (2019); Prause & Pfaus (2015)

sources.cite: Grubbs et al. (2019). Pornography problems due to moral incongruence: An integrative model with a systematic review and meta-analysis. Archives of Sexual Behavior, 48, 397–415.

contested_findings.name: TED-style single-study claims
contested_findings.note: Many TED talks present a single study as settled science; several of the most-watched psychology talks rest on effects that later shrank or vanished.
contested_findings.source: General caution; see the specific finding tagged on the video

contested_findings.name: Myers-Briggs (MBTI)
contested_findings.note: The MBTI has poor test-retest reliability and its dichotomies do not match how traits are distributed; personality psychologists use the Big Five instead.
contested_findings.source: Pittenger (1993, 2005); Stein & Swan (2019)

sources.cite: Stein & Swan (2019). Evaluating the validity of Myers-Briggs Type Indicator theory: A teaching tool and window into intuitive psychology. Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 13(2), e12434.

contested_findings.name: Rat Park
contested_findings.note: Rat Park's message (environment matters for addiction) is supported, but the original study was small, had confounds, and direct replications were mixed; it is not proof that addiction is 'just' about disconnection.
contested_findings.source: Petrie (1996); Gage & Sumnall (2019) Addiction

sources.cite: Gage & Sumnall (2019). Rat Park: How a rat paradise changed the narrative of addiction. Addiction, 114(5), 917–922.

contested_findings.name: Multiple intelligences
contested_findings.note: Gardner's intelligences lack empirical support as separate abilities; measured cognitive abilities correlate strongly (the g factor).
contested_findings.source: Waterhouse (2006); Visser, Ashton & Vernon (2006)

sources.cite: Visser, Ashton & Vernon (2006). Beyond g: Putting multiple intelligences theory to the test. Intelligence, 34(5), 487–502.

contested_findings.name: Polyvagal theory
contested_findings.note: Popular in trauma therapy, but its core physiological claims about the vagus nerve are contradicted by comparative neuroanatomy.
contested_findings.source: Grossman & Taylor (2007); Grossman (2023)

sources.cite: Grossman & Taylor (2007). Toward understanding respiratory sinus arrhythmia: Relations to cardiac vagal tone, evolution and biobehavioral functions. Biological Psychology, 74(2), 263–285.

contested_findings.name: 'Body keeps the score' / repressed memory claims
contested_findings.note: Trauma's effects are real, but repressed-then-recovered memory claims lack solid support and contributed to false accusations; memory researchers dispute 'body memory' framings.
contested_findings.source: Loftus (1993); Otgaar et al. (2019) Perspectives on Psychological Science

sources.cite: Otgaar et al. (2019). The return of the repressed: The persistent and problematic claims of long-forgotten trauma. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 14(6), 1072–1095.

contested_findings.name: Adult 'attachment styles' as fixed types
contested_findings.note: Attachment is continuous and changes over time; pop versions treating anxious/avoidant as fixed personality types overstate the research.
contested_findings.source: Fraley (2019) Annual Review of Psychology

sources.cite: Fraley, R. C. (2019). Attachment in adulthood: Recent developments, emerging debates, and future directions. Annual Review of Psychology, 70, 401–422.

contested_findings.name: Dopamine detox / 'dopamine fasting'
contested_findings.note: You cannot deplete or reset dopamine by avoiding pleasures; the useful part (reducing compulsive habits) has nothing to do with dopamine levels.
contested_findings.source: Critiques by addiction neuroscientists; Sepah's original proposal was behavioral, not neurochemical

contested_findings.name: Choice overload / paradox of choice
contested_findings.note: The famous jam-study effect (more options, fewer purchases) averages close to zero across studies; choice overload appears only under specific conditions such as time pressure or unfamiliar options.
contested_findings.source: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (2010) meta-analysis; Chernev, Böckenholt & Goodman (2015)

sources.cite: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (2010). Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload. Journal of Consumer Research, 37(3), 409–425.
Chernev, Böckenholt & Goodman (2015). Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 25(2), 333–358.

contested_findings.name: Announcing goals makes you less likely to achieve them
contested_findings.note: Rests on a few small studies by Gollwitzer and colleagues; later work found sharing goals with people whose opinion you value can increase commitment and performance.
contested_findings.source: Gollwitzer et al. (2009); Klein, Lount, Park & Polin (2020) JAPSP

sources.cite: Klein, Lount, Park & Polin (2020). When goals are known: The effects of audience relative status on goal commitment and performance. Journal of Applied Psychology, 105(4), 372–389.

contested_findings.name: Stress mindset (‘make stress your friend’)
contested_findings.note: Based mainly on an observational study where perceived stress predicted mortality only when people also believed stress was harmful; causality and the size of the effect remain unsettled.
contested_findings.source: Keller et al. (2012) Health Psychology; Crum, Salovey & Achor (2013)

sources.cite: Keller et al. (2012). Does the perception that stress affects health matter? The association with health and mortality. Health Psychology, 31(5), 677–684.

contested_findings.name: Asch conformity
contested_findings.note: The effect is real and has replicated for seventy years, but a meta-analysis of 133 studies found it shrank after the 1950s and is larger in collectivist cultures; most participants gave the right answer most of the time.
contested_findings.source: Bond & Smith (1996) Psychological Bulletin

sources.cite: Bond, R., & Smith, P. B. (1996). Culture and conformity: A meta-analysis of studies using Asch's (1952b, 1956) line judgment task. Psychological Bulletin, 119(1), 111–137.

contested_findings.name: Robbers Cave
contested_findings.note: Robbers Cave (1954) was Sherif's second attempt: the 1953 Middle Grove camp had failed when the boys united against the staff, and was dropped from the record. The 1954 conflict was more staged than the textbooks say.
contested_findings.source: Perry (2018) The Lost Boys; Sherif papers, Cummings Center

sources.cite: Perry, G. (2018). The Lost Boys: Inside Muzafer Sherif's Robbers Cave Experiment. Scribe.
Sherif, M., Harvey, O. J., White, B. J., Hood, W. R., & Sherif, C. W. (1961). Intergroup Conflict and Cooperation: The Robbers Cave Experiment. University Book Exchange.

contested_findings.name: Apes learning language (Washoe, Koko, Nim, Kanzi)
contested_findings.note: Terrace's analysis of Nim's signing found prompted, repetitive, non-syntactic strings, and Koko's claims were never fully documented; Kanzi's comprehension of spoken English is the strongest evidence. Apes learn symbols; whether they learn language depends on what you mean by language.
contested_findings.source: Terrace et al. (1979) Science; Savage-Rumbaugh et al. (1993)

sources.cite: Terrace, H. S., Petitto, L. A., Sanders, R. J., & Bever, T. G. (1979). Can an ape create a sentence? Science, 206(4421), 891–902.
Savage-Rumbaugh, E. S., et al. (1993). Language comprehension in ape and child. Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development, 58(3–4).

contested_findings.name: Universal facial expressions of basic emotion
contested_findings.note: Ekman's six universal expressions rest partly on forced-choice methods; with free labelling and in remote groups, recognition is weaker and context-dependent (a Trobriand "fear face" was read as threat). Expressions are more variable than the basic-emotion view, though not arbitrary.
contested_findings.source: Barrett et al. (2019) PSPI; Crivelli et al. (2016) PNAS; Russell (1994)

sources.cite: Barrett, L. F., Adolphs, R., Marsella, S., Martinez, A. M., & Pollak, S. D. (2019). Emotional expressions reconsidered. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 20(1), 1–68.
Crivelli, C., Russell, J. A., Jarillo, S., & Fernández-Dols, J.-M. (2016). The fear gasping face as a threat display in a Melanesian society. PNAS, 113(44), 12403–12407.
Russell, J. A. (1994). Is there universal recognition of emotion from facial expression? Psychological Bulletin, 115(1), 102–141.

contested_findings.name: Cognitive dissonance (induced compliance)
contested_findings.note: Dissonance reduction is one of psychology's best-supported ideas, but a 39-lab registered replication of the classic induced-compliance paradigm (write a counter-attitudinal essay for little reward) found no reliable attitude change. The theory stands; the textbook demonstration is shakier.
contested_findings.source: Vaidis et al. (2024) AMPPS; Festinger & Carlsmith (1959)

sources.cite: Vaidis, D. C., et al. (2024). A multisite preregistered paradigmatic test of the cognitive dissonance theory. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 7(1).
Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203–210.

contested_findings.name: Anchoring
contested_findings.note: One of the sturdiest effects in the field: Many Labs 1 replicated anchoring in all 36 samples across 12 countries, with effects as large as the originals.
contested_findings.source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs 1

sources.cite: Klein, R. A., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3), 142–152.
Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131.

contested_findings.name: Gain–loss framing (the Asian disease problem)
contested_findings.note: Tversky and Kahneman's framing effect replicated across Many Labs 1 and 2 (dozens of sites, thousands of participants) with little variation between cultures.
contested_findings.source: Klein et al. (2014, 2018) Many Labs 1 and 2

sources.cite: Klein, R. A., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443–490.
Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1981). The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice. Science, 211(4481), 453–458.

contested_findings.name: The bystander effect
contested_findings.note: In the lab, more bystanders means less and slower help, and a meta-analysis confirms it; but in 219 real CCTV-recorded conflicts in three countries, at least one bystander intervened 91% of the time, and more bystanders meant more chance of help.
contested_findings.source: Fischer et al. (2011) Psychological Bulletin; Philpot et al. (2020) American Psychologist

sources.cite: Fischer, P., et al. (2011). The bystander-effect: A meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies. Psychological Bulletin, 137(4), 517–537.

Philpot, R., Liebst, L. S., Levine, M., Bernasco, W., & Lindegaard, M. R. (2020). Would I be helped? Cross-national CCTV footage shows that intervention is the norm in public conflicts. American Psychologist, 75(1), 66–75.

contested_findings.name: The Macbeth effect (moral cleansing)
contested_findings.note: The finding that recalling an unethical act makes people want to wash did not survive three direct replications, and later meta-analysis puts the effect near zero.
contested_findings.source: Earp et al. (2014) Basic and Applied Social Psychology; Siev et al. (2018)

sources.cite: Earp, B. D., Everett, J. A. C., Madva, E. N., & Hamlin, J. K. (2014). Out, damned spot: Can the "Macbeth effect" be replicated? Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 36(1), 91–98.
Zhong, C.-B., & Liljenquist, K. (2006). Washing away your sins: Threatened morality and physical cleansing. Science, 313(5792), 1451–1452.

contested_findings.name: Terror management (mortality salience)
contested_findings.note: Many Labs 4 ran the flagship mortality-salience study (reminders of death make Americans favour pro-US essays) in 21 labs, with and without the original authors' involvement, and found no effect either way.
contested_findings.source: Klein et al. (2022) Many Labs 4, Collabra

sources.cite: Klein, R. A., et al. (2022). Many Labs 4: Failure to replicate mortality salience effect with and without original author involvement. Collabra: Psychology, 8(1), 35271.

contested_findings.name: Bem's precognition ("Feeling the Future")
contested_findings.note: The 2011 JPSP paper claiming people can sense future events failed preregistered replications and became the case study that started the replication crisis.
contested_findings.source: Ritchie, Wiseman & French (2012) PLOS ONE; Galak et al. (2012) JPSP

sources.cite: Ritchie, S. J., Wiseman, R., & French, C. C. (2012). Failing the future: Three unsuccessful attempts to replicate Bem's "retroactive facilitation of recall" effect. PLOS ONE, 7(3), e33423.
Galak, J., LeBoeuf, R. A., Nelson, L. D., & Simmons, J. P. (2012). Correcting the past: Failures to replicate psi. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(6), 933–948.

contested_findings.name: Hungry judges
contested_findings.note: The famous drop in parole approvals before lunch is largely explained by how cases were scheduled (prisoners without lawyers came last in each session), not by judges' blood sugar; the implied effect size was never plausible.
contested_findings.source: Weinshall-Margel & Shapard (2011) PNAS; Glöckner (2016)

sources.cite: Weinshall-Margel, K., & Shapard, J. (2011). Overlooked factors in the analysis of parole decisions. PNAS, 108(42), E833.
Danziger, S., Levav, J., & Avnaim-Pesso, L. (2011). Extraneous factors in judicial decisions. PNAS, 108(17), 6889–6892.

contested_findings.name: Oxytocin, the "love hormone"
contested_findings.note: The intranasal-oxytocin studies behind the "trust hormone" story (Kosfeld 2005) have not replicated; a review of the literature found no reliable effect on trust in healthy adults, and most studies were underpowered.
contested_findings.source: Nave, Camerer & McCullough (2015) Perspectives on Psychological Science

sources.cite: Nave, G., Camerer, C., & McCullough, M. (2015). Does oxytocin increase trust in humans? A critical review of research. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(6), 772–789.

contested_findings.name: Brain-training games make you smarter
contested_findings.note: People get better at the trained games; the gains do not transfer to untrained cognitive tasks or everyday functioning. A six-week trial of 11,000 people found no transfer, and a 2016 review found the industry's evidence did not meet basic standards.
contested_findings.source: Owen et al. (2010) Nature; Simons et al. (2016) PSPI

sources.cite: Simons, D. J., et al. (2016). Do "brain-training" programs work? Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 17(3), 103–186.
Owen, A. M., et al. (2010). Putting brain training to the test. Nature, 465, 775–778.

contested_findings.name: The bilingual advantage in executive function
contested_findings.note: Early studies reported sharper attention and inhibition in bilinguals; large samples and a meta-analysis correcting for publication bias find little or no advantage.
contested_findings.source: Paap & Greenberg (2013); Lehtonen et al. (2018) Psychological Bulletin

sources.cite: Lehtonen, M., et al. (2018). Is bilingualism associated with enhanced executive functioning in adults? A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 144(4), 394–425.
Paap, K. R., & Greenberg, Z. I. (2013). There is no coherent evidence for a bilingual advantage in executive processing. Cognitive Psychology, 66(2), 232–258.

contested_findings.name: Rosenhan's "On Being Sane in Insane Places"
contested_findings.note: Archival work found Rosenhan's own admission notes contradicted his account (he reported more symptoms than claimed), could not find most of the eight pseudopatients, and omitted one whose experience was positive. Asylum reform did not need the study, but it leaned on it.
contested_findings.source: Cahalan (2019) The Great Pretender

sources.cite: Cahalan, S. (2019). The Great Pretender: The Undercover Mission That Changed Our Understanding of Madness. Grand Central.
Rosenhan, D. L. (1973). On being sane in insane places. Science, 179(4070), 250–258.

contested_findings.name: Subliminal advertising ("Eat popcorn")
contested_findings.note: Vicary's 1957 cinema study never happened as described (he admitted it in 1962). Subliminal priming can nudge choices in tightly controlled lab conditions when people are already thirsty, which is a very different claim.
contested_findings.source: Pratkanis (1992); Karremans et al. (2006) JESP

sources.cite: Karremans, J. C., Stroebe, W., & Claus, J. (2006). Beyond Vicary's fantasies: The impact of subliminal priming and brand choice. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 42(6), 792–798.

contested_findings.name: We only use 10% of our brains
contested_findings.note: Imaging, lesion studies and metabolism all say otherwise: there is no dormant 90%, and damage almost anywhere costs something. The myth's origins are murky (misreadings of William James and early neuron counts).
contested_findings.source: Lilienfeld et al. (2010) 50 Great Myths of Popular Psychology

sources.cite: Lilienfeld, S. O., Lynn, S. J., Ruscio, J., & Beyerstein, B. L. (2010). 50 Great Myths of Popular Psychology. Wiley-Blackwell.

contested_findings.name: The hot-hand "fallacy"
contested_findings.note: The 1985 paper that declared basketball's hot hand an illusion contained a subtle selection bias; corrected, the original data show a real hot hand. A textbook case of the debunking being the thing that was wrong.
contested_findings.source: Miller & Sanjurjo (2018) Econometrica

sources.cite: Miller, J. B., & Sanjurjo, A. (2018). Surprised by the hot hand fallacy? A truth in the law of small numbers. Econometrica, 86(6), 2019–2047.
Gilovich, T., Vallone, R., & Tversky, A. (1985). The hot hand in basketball: On the misperception of random sequences. Cognitive Psychology, 17(3), 295–314.

contested_findings.name: Birth order shapes personality
contested_findings.note: In three national samples totalling more than 20,000 people, birth order had no effect on the Big Five traits (a small first-born advantage in IQ remains).
contested_findings.source: Rohrer, Egloff & Schmukle (2015) PNAS

sources.cite: Rohrer, J. M., Egloff, B., & Schmukle, S. C. (2015). Examining the effects of birth order on personality. PNAS, 112(46), 14224–14229.

contested_findings.name: Teacher expectations (Pygmalion in the classroom)
contested_findings.note: Expectation effects on students exist but are small, mostly dissipate, and teacher expectations are mostly accurate; the dramatic 1968 claims came from a few odd data points.
contested_findings.source: Jussim & Harber (2005) Personality and Social Psychology Review

sources.cite: Jussim, L., & Harber, K. D. (2005). Teacher expectations and self-fulfilling prophecies: Knowns and unknowns, resolved and unresolved controversies. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 9(2), 131–155.

contested_findings.name: Mindfulness as a cure-all
contested_findings.note: Meta-analysis finds moderate benefits for anxiety, depression and pain, comparable to other active treatments, and no good evidence for many broader claims; much of the literature is small, unblinded and poorly controlled.
contested_findings.source: Goyal et al. (2014) JAMA Internal Medicine; Van Dam et al. (2018) "Mind the hype"

sources.cite: Goyal, M., et al. (2014). Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: A systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine, 174(3), 357–368.
Van Dam, N. T., et al. (2018). Mind the hype: A critical evaluation and prescriptive agenda for research on mindfulness and meditation. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 13(1), 36–61.

contested_findings.name: Microexpressions reveal lies
contested_findings.note: Microexpressions are rare, appear in truth-tellers too, and human lie detection averages 54% in meta-analysis; training programs built on them have not shown reliable gains.
contested_findings.source: Porter & ten Brinke (2008) Psychological Science; Bond & DePaulo (2006)

sources.cite: Porter, S., & ten Brinke, L. (2008). Reading between the lies: Identifying concealed and falsified emotions in universal facial expressions. Psychological Science, 19(5), 508–514.
Bond, C. F., & DePaulo, B. M. (2006). Accuracy of deception judgments. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 10(3), 214–234.

contested_findings.name: Eye direction reveals lying (NLP)
contested_findings.note: The neuro-linguistic programming claim that liars look up and to the right failed three tests, including one with real high-stakes appeals.
contested_findings.source: Wiseman et al. (2012) PLOS ONE

sources.cite: Wiseman, R., Watt, C., ten Brinke, L., Porter, S., Couper, S.-L., & Rankin, C. (2012). The eyes don't have it: Lie detection and neuro-linguistic programming. PLOS ONE, 7(7), e40259.

contested_findings.name: Violent media causes aggression
contested_findings.note: From the Bobo doll on, lab studies find short-term imitation; whether games and film raise real-world violence is disputed, with competing meta-analyses finding small effects or none once publication bias is corrected.
contested_findings.source: Anderson et al. (2010) vs Ferguson & Kilburn (2010), Psychological Bulletin

sources.cite: Anderson, C. A., et al. (2010). Violent video game effects on aggression, empathy, and prosocial behavior in Eastern and Western countries: A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 136(2), 151–173.

Ferguson, C. J., & Kilburn, J. (2010). Much ado about nothing: The misestimation and overinterpretation of violent video game effects in Eastern and Western nations. Psychological Bulletin, 136(2), 174–178.

contested_findings.name: Inattentional blindness (the gorilla)
contested_findings.note: Holds up everywhere it has been tried: half of people miss the gorilla, expert radiologists miss one embedded in a CT scan, and knowing the trick does not protect you from the next unexpected event.
contested_findings.source: Simons (2010) i-Perception; Drew, Võ & Wolfe (2013) Psychological Science

sources.cite: Drew, T., Võ, M. L.-H., & Wolfe, J. M. (2013). The invisible gorilla strikes again: Sustained inattentional blindness in expert observers. Psychological Science, 24(9), 1848–1853.
Simons, D. J. (2010). Monkeying around with the gorillas in our midst. i-Perception, 1(1), 3–6.

contested_findings.name: The McGurk effect
contested_findings.note: Forty years of replication: the illusion is robust, though its strength varies between individuals and languages (weaker in Japanese and Chinese listeners).
contested_findings.source: Alsius, Paré & Munhall (2018) Multisensory Research

sources.cite: Alsius, A., Paré, M., & Munhall, K. G. (2018). Forty years after Hearing Lips and Seeing Voices: The McGurk effect revisited. Multisensory Research, 31(1–2), 111–144.

contested_findings.name: The rubber hand illusion
contested_findings.note: The illusion replicates reliably and has an fMRI signature, but a 2020 study found that much of the self-report correlates with hypnotic suggestibility and expectations, so part of what people report may be demand characteristics.
contested_findings.source: Ehrsson et al. (2004) Science; Lush et al. (2020) Nature Communications

sources.cite: Lush, P., et al. (2020). Trait phenomenological control predicts experience of mirror synaesthesia and the rubber hand illusion. Nature Communications, 11, 4853.
Ehrsson, H. H., Spence, C., & Passingham, R. E. (2004). That's my hand! Activity in premotor cortex reflects feeling of ownership of a limb. Science, 305(5685), 875–877.

contested_findings.name: The Stroop effect
contested_findings.note: Among the most reliable effects in experimental psychology, reproduced in essentially every sample since 1935; the argument is about mechanism, not existence.
contested_findings.source: MacLeod (1991) Psychological Bulletin

sources.cite: MacLeod, C. M. (1991). Half a century of research on the Stroop effect: An integrative review. Psychological Bulletin, 109(2), 163–203.

contested_findings.name: Split-brain patients have two minds
contested_findings.note: The classic demonstrations are real, but a 2017 re-examination found split-brain patients could respond to stimuli anywhere in the visual field with either hand and verbally, suggesting one agent with divided perception rather than two separate conscious selves.
contested_findings.source: Pinto et al. (2017) Brain

sources.cite: Pinto, Y., et al. (2017). Split brain: Divided perception but undivided consciousness. Brain, 140(5), 1231–1237.

contested_findings.name: Learned helplessness
contested_findings.note: The dogs were real; the mechanism was backwards. Fifty years on, Maier and Seligman concluded that passivity in the face of shock is the default mammalian response, and what is learned is control — the opposite of the original story.
contested_findings.source: Maier & Seligman (2016) Psychological Review

sources.cite: Maier, S. F., & Seligman, M. E. P. (2016). Learned helplessness at fifty: Insights from neuroscience. Psychological Review, 123(4), 349–367.

contested_findings.name: Pavlov's bell
contested_findings.note: Pavlov used metronomes, buzzers, harmoniums and electric shocks far more than bells; the bell is largely a translation artefact. His dogs also did not simply "drool at a sound" — he was mapping the nervous system.
contested_findings.source: Todes (2014) Ivan Pavlov: A Russian Life in Science; Tully (2003) Current Biology

sources.cite: Tully, T. (2003). Pavlov's dogs. Current Biology, 13(4), R117–R119.
Black, S. L. (2003). Pavlov's dogs: For whom the bell rarely tolled. Current Biology, 13(11), R426.
Todes, D. P. (2014). Ivan Pavlov: A Russian Life in Science. Oxford University Press.

contested_findings.name: Phineas Gage, "no longer Gage"
contested_findings.note: The personality-change story rests on a few lines from one physician; Gage later held a skilled job as a stagecoach driver in Chile for years, which suggests substantial recovery that the textbooks leave out.
contested_findings.source: Macmillan (2000) An Odd Kind of Fame; Macmillan & Lena (2010)

sources.cite: Macmillan, M., & Lena, M. L. (2010). Rehabilitating Phineas Gage. Neuropsychological Rehabilitation, 20(5), 641–658.
